claim: CVE-2025-53773 allowed RCE via prompt injection in GitHub Copilot by injecting content that makes the agent write 'chat.tools.autoApprove': true into .vscode/settings.json, disabling all user confirmations.
quote: The prompt injection first adds the line 'chat.tools.autoApprove': true, to the ~/.vscode/settings.json file.

claim: CodeRabbit states it does not retain source code after review (except when caching is enabled), never uses code for training, and is SOC 2 Type II certified and GDPR compliant.
quote: CodeRabbit does not retain your source code after a review completes, except when review caching is enabled... encrypted, used only to accelerate reviews, never used for training, and expires automatically... CodeRabbit is SOC Type II certified and GDPR compliant

claim: The 'Comment and Control' attack (disclosed April 2026, Aonan Guan et al.) used HTML-comment-hidden instructions in PR titles/issue comments to make Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and GitHub Copilot Agent leak credentials including GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_COPILOT_API_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and GEMINI_API_KEY.
quote: The attacker creates a GitHub issue with a visible request and hidden instructions in an HTML comment ... GitHub Actions workflows fire automatically on pull_request, issues, and issue_comment events, so simply opening a PR or filing an issue can trigger the AI agent without any action from the victim.

claim: Greptile is SOC2 Type II compliant, stores encrypted customer code until GitHub/GitLab access is revoked, and may use de-identified customer data for AI training unless the customer opts out; on-prem and bring-your-own-LLM options exist.
quote: Greptile may use de-identified customer data for AI training purposes ... If you do not wish to permit Greptile to engage in AI training, you may manage preferences and settings related to AI training within your account on the Platform.

claim: Three widely deployed AI coding agents were confirmed vulnerable to a single prompt-injection class with no external server needed; Anthropic rated its issue CVSS 9.4 Critical but paid only a $100 bounty.
quote: an attacker writes a malicious PR title or issue comment, the AI agent reads and processes it as trusted context, executes attacker-supplied instructions, and exfiltrates credentials back through a PR comment, issue comment, or git commit, no external server required.

claim: The CamoLeak attack hid prompts in PR descriptions and abused GitHub's Camo image proxy to exfiltrate AWS keys and private-repo data one character at a time; Legit Security's Omer Mayraz disclosed it and GitHub fixed it by disabling image rendering in Copilot Chat.
quote: hidden content that never appears when rendered by GitHub as HTML because it is ignored by the Markdown parser ... GitHub fixed it by disabling image rendering in Copilot Chat completely

claim: CamoLeak was tracked as CVE-2025-59145 with a CVSS score of 9.6, allowing silent theft of source code, API keys and secrets (including AWS keys and private zero-day descriptions) from private repositories via GitHub Copilot Chat.
quote: source code, API keys, and secrets from private repositories ... demonstration showed successful theft of AWS keys and privately stored zero-day vulnerability descriptions

claim: Effective April 24 2026, GitHub Copilot inputs, outputs and code snippets from Free/Pro/Pro+ tiers may be used for model training by default (opt-out), while Copilot Business and Enterprise are exempt.
quote: Copilot inputs, outputs, code snippets, and associated context may now be used for model training ... This is an opt-out policy. The setting defaults to enabled ... Covered (affected): Copilot Free, Pro, and Pro+ ... Exempt: Copilot Business, Copilot Enterprise

claim: Orca Security's RoguePilot (disclosed early 2026) exploited the integration between GitHub Issues and the in-Codespaces Copilot agent to achieve full repository takeover with no direct attacker interaction.

Autonomous coding agents introduce supply-chain attack surface including tool/plugin poisoning, privilege escalation and cascading failures, with compromised agent plugins presenting as feature updates rather than malware.
quote: Autonomous agents introduce emerging risks, including prompt injection and manipulation, tool misuse and privilege escalation, memory poisoning, cascading failures, and supply chain attacks.
